residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0373) BY A RESIDENCY TEST, NOT BY A TRADE. T-0376's pass mints the register's `new_resident` people whose trade the papers print; this one takes the rest, where there is no trade to anchor anybody and a printed name on its own proves only that a Chicago paper set the type. The test asks the corpus two questions instead: does it place this person inside the town and NOWHERE outside it, and does a second independent witness corroborate a bare 'Chicago' — an address at street level, print in two or more issues, or print beside two or more people this reconstruction already holds. THE CORPUS GIVES AN ADDRESS IN THE TOWN — Lake Street — which is a placement no visitor passing through acquires. The household around them is a CONTAINER and not an argument: one member, no dwelling, no division, no family, no recorded trade, and every one of those absences written as unattested rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. That the person is a HOUSEHOLD is the one invention here and it is recorded as docs/LIBERTIES.md L213. tools/mint_placed_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

persons.name: Clark Knight
persons.note: THE LADDER'S OWN READING OF THIS EVIDENCE. Read from newspaper_letter_list, poll_1834. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1c), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1834 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Knight, Clark” (poll_1834_069, line 238). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Knight' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1a), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1835 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1835 and nothing says when they came. THE BOUND FALLS AFTER THE SCENE DATE and the record says so rather than narrowing it: the earliest source that names this person is later than 1 July 1835, so they may have arrived after the day this scene models. present_on_scene_date is `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “John Knight” (33SQ-GYYJ-93G, printed page 207, line 21). This project has ruled the head a CANDIDATE and no more: the name agrees and is unique on both sides, but nothing independent of the name was found. A candidate is not an identity — nothing is asserted from it, no household of 1840 is carried back, and the ruling is recorded so that a reader can see it was made rather than missed. Under the rule that decided it (L7 candidate), by the crosswalk's own ladder (data/research/census_1840/resident_crosswalk.json). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of 1835 — “Knight, John” (poll_1835_043, line 330). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Knight' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

persons.name: Mrs. C. Taylor
persons.note:
A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER PRINTS THIS WOMAN BY NAME, IN THE TOWN, KEEPING A HOUSE ON WATER STREET. The Chicago Democrat of 19 August 1835, page 3 column 2, over copy dated Chicago, 10 August 1835: "The Ladies and Gen[t]lemen of the town of Chicago are respec[t]fully in[v]ited to attend a sale of the \"Juvenile Society's\" work, [at] 3 o'clock P.[M.] next Saturday, the 22d inst., at the hous[e] of Mrs. C. Taylor, Water-st." THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER (T-0513), rung G1b: an 1833-1835 newspaper naming the person in Chicago is `attested` on its own, and this printing names her, the town and her house at once.

WHY THE TOWN HAD NO CARD FOR HER, WHICH IS A FINDING ABOUT THE RULES AND NOT ABOUT HER. Her one appearance is not missing from the research tree — it is SPENT ON A MAN. data/research/residents/identity_master.json folds `person_taylor_mrs_c` into `id_taylor_charles` and grading_proposal.json lists it among that identity's evidence. R6 (T-0723, #998) exists to stop exactly this — "a wife is not her husband and never merges onto him" — but it is EXACT-MATCH ONLY by design: it fires where the honorific strip leaves the husband's forename tokens letter for letter, as `Mrs. Rufus B. Brown` does against `Brown, Rufus B.` Here the printed forename is an INITIAL. Stripped of "Mrs." the reading is `Taylor, C.`, which is not identical to `Taylor, Charles`, so R6 never looks at it and M2 does — "an initial-only forename attaches to the ONE full forename of that surname carrying the initial" — and the one C-forename Taylor in the corpus is Charles. A female honorific carrying an initial is the shape R6 cannot see. The finding is recorded on T-0951, which already owns the two husband-name printings R6 cannot reach.

IS SHE THE WIFE OF A TAYLOR THE TOWN ALREADY HOLDS? ASKED, AND THE ANSWER IS NO ON THE EVIDENCE HELD. `data/residents/households/` carries five Taylor heads — Anson H., Augustine Deodat, Edmund D, William and William H — and not one of them has a forename beginning with C, so under the period's own usage ("Mrs. C. Taylor" is the wife of a man whose forename begins with C) she is the wife of NONE OF THE FIVE HEADS. The only C-forename Taylor this project holds is Charles H. Taylor, and he is not a head: he is Anson's brother inside hh_taylor_anson. Whether she was HIS wife is not decided by anything in this dataset. R6's own standard is that a source must print both readings, and no source prints `Taylor, Charles` and `Taylor, Mrs. C.` as two entries of one list — the Democrat prints them in different issues, six weeks apart, about different things. The one place a wife of a Charles Taylor is named at all is data/structures/wolf_point_tavern.json, which has "Charles and Mary Taylor" keeping that house 1831-1833; hh_taylor_anson's own note REFUSES that identification outright, on the ground that the Taylor surname is carried by at least four distinct men in these sources. So no kin[] row is written here, and the absence is the finding: she stands as her own resident, which is what R6 would have done for her had it been able to see her.

ONE LATER RECORD THE CROSSWALK NOW REACHES, AND IT IS NOT AN 1835 FACT. Rebuilding data/research/church/second_presbyterian_crosswalk.json against this card matched it to a single roll line — `second_presb_0870`, printed page 203, as read: "Taylor, Mrs. Charle's | Letter. | Januarys, 1843. | Dismissed." (the date token is the transcription's, unrepaired; the crosswalk reads the year as 1843). A woman entered on that roll under a man's forename, admitted by letter and afterwards dismissed. It says that the honorific shape read here is the shape this town's own paper used, and it is corroboration of nothing else: the roll is of 1842-1892, the ladder binds an 1843 appearance to CONTINUED RESIDENCE at best, and the town holds two men it could stand on — Charles H. Taylor the currier and the Charles Taylor Fergus 1843 prints as a merchant tailor on Clark Street. The match is left where the crosswalk put it, PROPOSED AND UNSPENT: no identity is asserted, the grade does not move, and this card cites the Democrat alone. 

WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the woman, her house's street and the source — no structure, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. No figure is drawn (L1). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Taylor, Mrs. Charle's | Letter. | Januarys, 1843. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0895, printed page 203), admitted 1843 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Taylor' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins C. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. THE SAME ROLL LINE IS MET BY OTHER TOWNSPEOPLE OF THIS NAME: second_presb_0895 is matched under this same rule to Charles H. Taylor (taylor_charles), so it is met by two townspeople of this name, and it says which of them it was about no more than it says it was about this one — the test that decided it is a surname and a given initial agreeing, which cannot tell them apart. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

residents.research_note: HAND-AUTHORED, NOT MINTED (T-0960). The three mint tools did not produce this card and could not have: the consolidation that feeds them folds this woman's only printing onto Charles Taylor by M2, so no identity of her own ever reached them — see the head's note. The card is written directly from the transcription in data/research/newspapers/extracted/chicago_democrat_1835_08_19.json, claim c007, which is on `dev` and unspent: no household in data/residents/ cites that locator or that record id. Nothing is taken off `taylor_charles` by writing this, because his card never cited the Democrat — his sources are Andreas, the IRAD poll lists, the land tract register and the 1840 census. THE SALVAGE: #925 wrote a version of this card and was never landed (its branch closed with T-0723 under #998); this one keeps its grade, rung and `uncertain` presence, dates the bound from the notice's own copy date rather than the printing date, and replaces its `lives_at` note — which read "the lists that name this person give no address" — with the street the notice actually gives.

what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.

District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.
A required distinction between named documentary landmarks and anonymous inferred infill.
what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

fabric_basis.words: silvered clapboard on a braced frame, 9-over-6 sash of 6 × 8 in glass, plain corner boards and a stoop, under a weather-darkened roof — a small two-story frame house, from the 1832–33 town (rule F-T: a tradesman's by its type)
